prose.def: Vapor, steam, or mist — in Acts a rising column of smoky vapor as an apocalyptic sign; in James a fleeting mist illustrating life's brevity.

It appears just twice in the New Testament: in Acts 2:19 it describes "vapor of smoke" (quoting the Septuagint), and in James 4:14 a human life is compared to a mist that appears briefly and then vanishes. prose.def: An indivisible instant of time—a moment so brief it cannot be divided or split.
prose.article: Built from a negative prefix and the root meaning "to cut" (G5114), ἄτομος literally means "uncuttable" or "indivisible," and is the source of our word "atom." In its single New Testament appearance (1 Corinthians 15:52), it describes time, naming an instant too small to divide—which the Majority Standard Bible renders "twinkling" 100% of the time, with the KJV using "moment." Moulton-Milligan note a striking parallel in Symmachus's version of Isaiah 54:8, "ἐν ἀτόμῳ ὀργῆς" (in a moment of wrath), suggesting Paul may have drawn the word from everyday Koine rather than directly from Plato or Aristotle.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single occurrence.

prose.def: Out of place: describing conduct as improper, wicked, or unreasonable, and in one usage describing something strange or harmful.
prose.article: At its root ἄτοπος means "out of place" (from a negative prefix plus τόπος, "place"), and from there it developed an ethical sense of improper, unrighteous, or perverse. In the New Testament it usually carries this moral meaning, as when Paul asks to be delivered from "wicked" people in 2 Thessalonians 3:2, though in Acts 28:6 it describes Paul suffering no "harm" after a snakebite. The Septuagint uses it 7 times and consistently in the ethical sense, most often translating the Hebrew word אָוֶן (āwen), meaning iniquity or wickedness; the classical lexica note that Plato favored a different shade entirely, using it for what is marvellous or odd.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only 3 occurrences in the Byzantine text and just 1 rendered with its own English word — so the range here is mapped more from the Septuagint and lexica than from measured New Testament usage.

prose.def: Babylon, the ancient city on the Euphrates where Jerusalem's people were exiled, and a symbolic name for a great oppressive power.
prose.article: Βαβυλών is the proper name Babylon, rendered "Babylon" in 10 of its 12 New Testament appearances (91%). It points literally to the ancient city on the Euphrates—the place of Israel's exile—but several reference works note it also functions symbolically: Abbott-Smith and Dodson take many Revelation passages, and probably 1 Peter 5:13, as standing for Rome. The name comes from Hebrew בָּבֶל, which the Septuagint renders with this Greek form 120 times, and it even shows up in everyday papyri, including a second-century letter instructing that camels be sent to Babylon.
prose.caution: Sources agree on the literal sense but differ on which passages are symbolic, so the figurative use of "Babylon" for Rome is interpretive rather than measured.

prose.article: Literally a βαθμός is a step or stair, but in its single New Testament appearance (1 Timothy 3:13) it carries the figurative sense of a standing or rank one achieves. The Septuagint uses it six times, including for the steps of a sundial in 2 Kings 20, and it shows up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions. One inscription from Mytilene uses the related form for someone who proved worthy of an honorable office, which fits the idea of gaining good standing in 1 Timothy.
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the evidence base is thin, so its exact shade of meaning is somewhat uncertain.

prose.def: The depth or profound extent of something, whether literal deep water, an extreme degree of a condition, or the unfathomable mystery of God's wisdom and counsels.
prose.article: βάθος names the measurable reach of something downward or inward — the deep part of a lake, the depth of soil, or the boundless extent of God's wisdom. In the New Testament it appears 8 times, rendered "depth" in half the cases and "deep" in a third, with two uses absorbed into surrounding phrasing. The everyday roots of the word show up in the papyri, where it describes digging a trench "to a depth" and setting plants into garden furrows, and in the Septuagint it often translates Hebrew words for the lowest places or the ocean depths.
prose.caution: The figurative senses (such as the "depth" of God's riches) sit alongside plain physical depth, so context decides which is meant.

prose.def: To dig deep (go deep into the ground), describing a builder's excavation before laying a foundation; English Bibles often render the surrounding clause as 'flood.'
prose.article: βαθύνω comes from βαθύς ("deep") and means to deepen or dig down, picturing the careful work of excavating before building. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Luke 6:48, where a wise builder digs deep to set a foundation on rock; the Majority Standard Bible renders it "flood" there, though the verb itself describes the deepening, not the flood. Interestingly, the Septuagint uses it just three times, and Moulton-Milligan note it is rare enough that they could point to only a single comparable instance (Philo) of this transitive verb being used to mean "go deep."
prose.caution: This is a New Testament hapax with very thin attestation, and the lexical sources ("to deepen, dig deep") do not match the measured rendering "flood," so the meaning rests on sparse evidence.
